s: The Discourse is heard by Sudharman from the Venerable Mahâvîra and concerns the enumeration and explanation of the twenty-two troubles. It teaches how a monk should bear and conquer each trouble.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: The unit concerns the Four Requisites: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control. It describes living beings wandering through Samsâra in various births according to their actions, suffering until cessation of Karman may lead them to human birth. Those who obtain the four requisites can practice penances and self-control, shake off sinfulness, and reach the highest Nirvâna as an eternal Siddha. It also describes Yakshas dwelling in the upper Kalpa heavens before descending and being born as men.

l: The Four Requisites, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: The Four Requisites are human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control. They are difficult for a living being to obtain.

l: human birth, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: Human birth is difficult to obtain. By the cessation of Karman, living beings may in due time become men.

l: instruction in the Law, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: Instruction in the Law is difficult to obtain even for those born with a human body. Hearing it enables beings to do penances, combat their passions, and abstain from killing living beings.

l: belief in the Law, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: Belief in the Law is difficult to obtain even after hearing it, because many who are shown the right way stray from it.

l: energy in self-control, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: Energy in self-control is difficult to fulfill strenuously, even for those who have heard and believed in the Law. Many who approve of the religion do not adopt it.

l: living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: Living beings are born in different families, castes, and forms according to their actions. They undergo misery in non-human births, but through cessation of Karman may eventually be born as men.

Samsâra contains recurring births in which living beings become gods, hell-beings, Asuras, Kshattriyas, Kandâlas, Bukkasas, worms, moths, Kunthu, or ants. Living beings are not disgusted with Samsâra despite its recurring misery.
The Law is difficult to hear, believe in, and fulfill. Those who hear and believe in it may practice penances, combat their passions, abstain from killing living beings, and stand firmly in it.
Penances help beings shake off the remnant of Karman. An ascetic who performs them after obtaining the Four Requisites can reach the highest Nirvâna.
Self-control is to be applied by one who has been born as a man, heard the Law, and believed in it. It restrains the ascetic and helps shake off sinfulness.
An ascetic who has obtained human birth, heard and believed in the Law, and fulfills it strenuously should restrain himself and shake off sinfulness.

l: the highest Nirvâna, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: The highest Nirvâna is reached by the soul after purity and firm standing in the Law. The soul reaches it like a fire fed with ghee.
A being who perceives that the Four Requisites are difficult to obtain, applies himself to self-control, and shakes off the remnant of Karman through penances becomes an eternal Siddha.

Yakshas gifted with various virtues live in heavenly regions situated one above the other. They enjoy divine pleasures, change their form at will, remain according to their merit, and later descend to be born as men.

l: the upper Kalpa heavens, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: The upper Kalpa heavens are regions where Yakshas live for many centuries of former years. There they enjoy divine pleasures and change their form at will.

Men are of ten kinds. Those born into families possessing fields and houses, gold, cattle, slaves, and servants may have good family, fine complexion, health, wisdom, nobility, fame, and power, and after enjoying human pleasures may obtain true knowledge.

l: true knowledge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Third Lecture.
s: True knowledge is obtained by a man through pure religious merit acquired in a former life, after he has enjoyed the unrivalled pleasures of human life at their proper time.

Karman causes living beings to be born in different forms and to undergo misery. When Karman ceases, beings may reach a pure state and be born as men; when its remnant is shaken off through penances, they may become an eternal Siddha.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourth Lecture.
s: The Fourth Lecture, titled Impurity, concerns the dangers of carelessness and the consequences of passions and actions. It teaches that human life is limited, wealth cannot protect the careless, and people cannot escape the effects of their own actions. It instructs a monk to remain watchful, conquer the will, avoid delusion and greed, and seek liberation through disciplined conduct. It also contrasts the impurity of heretics with the virtues a person should desire throughout life.

l: Fourth Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourth Lecture.
s: The Fourth Lecture teaches about impurity, carelessness, the consequences of actions, and the discipline required for liberation.
Impurity is associated with wrong principles, passions, delusion, deceit, greed, and heretics.
Carelessness leaves people without protection and unable to benefit from having seen the right way. A person should never be careless because life is limited and the body is weak.

l: human life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourth Lecture.
s: Human life cannot be prolonged and is not eternal. A person who delays conquering the will may despair when life draws to its close.
Wealth acquired through evil deeds will be lost, and wealth cannot protect a careless person in this world or the next.
Passions ensnare people and subject them to hatred, love, and other harmful influences.
People cannot escape the effects of their own actions. Relations will not come to a person's aid when that person reaps the fruits of actions performed for others or for personal benefit.

A monk should walk and live carefully, remain watchful, control himself, avoid hatred toward external things, and remove delusion, pride, deceit, and greed. By conquering the will and guarding himself, a monk can quickly obtain liberation.
Enlightenment is described as the stake a monk seeks after first taking care of his life and then annihilating his sins.
Conquering the will leads to liberation. Delaying victory over the will is dangerous because human life may end before it is achieved.
Liberation is reached by conquering the will and by remaining watchful, especially during one's young years.
A person living in the Samsâra cannot escape the effects of personal actions.
A Sramana who repeatedly suppresses delusion and controls himself is affected roughly by external things, but should not hate them in his mind.
Delusion should be kept away and repeatedly suppressed. External things weaken the intellect and allure many through delusion.

l: external things, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourth Lecture.
s: External things weaken the intellect and allure many. They may affect a monk roughly, but he should not hate them in his mind.
Heretics are described as impure and vain, always subject to love and hate, and wholly under the influence of their passions.

l: good actions, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourth Lecture.
s: A person should desire virtues until the end of life, while despising heretics as unholy men.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: The unit contrasts death against one's will, suffered by ignorant men repeatedly, with death with one's will, attained by wise men at most once. It describes how attachment to pleasures leads ignorant men to cruelty, sin, fear, remorse, hell, and rebirth according to their deeds. It teaches that virtuous monks and householders who practise self-control, penance, and the Law can meet death calmly and attain heavenly regions or liberation. A wise man chooses the better death through the Law of Compassion and prepares for the dissolution of the body without fear or joy.

l: death against one's will, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: Death against one's will is the death of ignorant men, and it happens to the same individual many times. It comes when a fool dies in fear after transgressing the Law and embracing unrighteousness.

l: death with one's will, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: Death with one's will is the death of wise men and at best happens only once. A sage dies this death according to one of three methods when the time for quitting the body has come.
Mahâvîra describes the death against one's will as the death of an ignorant man attached to pleasures who does cruel actions.

l: wise people, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: Wise men experience death with one's will, which is full of peace and free from injury to anyone. They weigh both kinds of death and choose the better one taught in the Law of Compassion.

l: ignorant men, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: Ignorant men are attached to pleasures and amusements and may kill, lie, deceive, calumniate, dissemble, drink liquor, and eat meat. They accumulate sins, suffer illness and fear, repent at death, and undergo death against one's will.
Sin is accumulated through overbearing acts and words, desire for wealth and women, and cruel or deceitful conduct. A sinful ascetic does not escape hell.
Hell is described as a place where fools who do cruel deeds suffer violently. A sinner, even if a mendicant, will not escape it.

The Law is transgressed by the fool who embraces unrighteousness, leading to remorse at the hour of death. A faithful man should practise the rules of conduct for householders and not neglect the Pôsaha fast.

l: virtuous man, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: The virtuous control themselves and subdue their senses, and they do not tremble at the hour of death. Through discipline they can attain heavenly regions or liberation.

Monks do not all possess good morality, and outward marks such as bark, skin, nakedness, twisted hair, or baldness do not save a sinful ascetic. Restrained monks become either free from all misery or gods of great power.

Householders have morality of various character, and some householders are superior to some monks in self-control. A faithful householder should follow the rules of conduct and observe the Pôsaha fast in both fortnights; living piously, he may share the world of the Yakshas.

Self-control is practised by those who control themselves and subdue their senses. Saints are superior to all householders in self-control, and those trained in self-control and penance may attain high regions or liberation.
Liberation is obtained by absence of passion. Those trained in self-control and penance, whether monks or householders, can attain liberation.

l: Law of Compassion, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifth Lecture.
s: The Law of Compassion teaches the better kind of death. A wise man who chooses it becomes calm through patience and keeps an undisturbed mind at death.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixth Lecture.
s: The False Ascetic concerns the suffering caused by ignorance of the Truth and the conduct required to escape bondage and birth in Samsâra. It teaches that a wise man should seek the truth, show kindness to all creatures, renounce possessions and attachments, avoid accepting presents, and sustain his body only to annihilate Karman. Merely attending a teacher or speaking about liberation without abstaining from sins and acting accordingly does not bring salvation. Arhat Gñâtriputra teaches that an ascetic should wander carefully, without a fixed residence or stored provisions, receiving permitted food in his alms-bowl while awaiting death.

l: The False Ascetic, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixth Lecture.
s: The False Ascetic is concerned with those who acknowledge bondage and liberation in words but do not abstain from sins or act according to their beliefs. Such people seek comfort in mighty words and mistakenly believe themselves wise while sinking through their sins.
Ignorance of the Truth subjects men to pain. A wise man should search for the truth and take it to heart.
All men who are ignorant of the Truth are subject to pain. People suffer for their own deeds, and those attached to their bodies, colours, and forms will reap pains.
In the endless Samsâra, ignorant men suffer in many ways. Those who remain attached to their bodies and sins travel a long way in Samsâra.
A wise man considers the ways that lead to bondage and birth. Recognising the truth about bondage and liberation, he should choose what is beyond and above this world.
A man should be kind towards all creatures and should not deprive them of life. Knowing creatures' love of their own self, he should cease endangering and combating them.
An ascetic should eat only the food put in his own alms-bowl to preserve his life. He should wander without desires, keeping no store, not even grease sticking to the alms-bowl.
Abstaining from sins is necessary for liberation; merely attending a teacher does not deliver a person from misery. Fools who continue through their sins believe themselves wise.

Liberation is acknowledged as the opposite of bondage, but talking about it without acting accordingly does not bring salvation. One should choose liberation over worldly objects and sustain the body only to annihilate Karman.
An ascetic should sustain his body only so that he can annihilate his Karman. Recognising the cause of Karman, he should wander about while awaiting death.

l: food and drink, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixth Lecture.
s: An ascetic should know the permitted quantity of food and drink. He should eat food prepared by householders for their own consumption and receive alms while avoiding faults.

l: Arhat Gñâtriputra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixth Lecture.
s: Arhat Gñâtriputra, the venerable native of Vaisâlî, speaks these teachings. He possesses the highest knowledge and the highest faith.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: The Seventh Lecture presents the Parable of the Ram and compares a ram raised for a guest with an ignorant great sinner who pursues pleasures and commits sins. It teaches that human life is capital, while gain represents heaven and loss of capital leads to hell or rebirth as a brute animal. The unit contrasts human pleasures with divine pleasures and the paths of the sinner and the virtuous man under the Law. It concludes that renouncing pleasure and following the true Law leads toward a godly state.

l: Seventh Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: The Seventh Lecture teaches through parables that human life is precious capital and that conduct determines whether one reaches heaven, hell, or another state.

l: Parable of the Ram, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: The Parable of the Ram compares an animal raised for a guest and then killed with an ignorant great sinner who lives for pleasures but gains life in hell.
The ram is raised, fed, and fattened for the arrival of a guest. When the guest arrives, its head is cut off and it is eaten.
The guest is the person for whose arrival the ram is raised and prepared. Its arrival causes the ram to be killed and eaten.

l: ignorant great sinner, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: The ignorant great sinner kills living beings, tells lies, robs, steals, deceives, pursues women and pleasures, drinks liquor, eats meat, and commits many sins. At death, under the burden of his Karman, he is grieved and falls to the world of the Asuras, to the dark place, or is born in hell.

l: virtuous man, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: The virtuous man turns away from unrighteousness and follows the true Law. He is born as a god and cheerfully attains the state of gods.

l: human life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: Human life is compared with capital entrusted to a merchant. It may be brought back through virtue, increased through eminent virtue, or lost through sinful conduct.
Capital represents human life. Bringing back the capital represents rebirth as a man, while increasing it represents attaining the state of gods.
Gain represents heaven in the parable of the three merchants.

l: loss of capital, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: Loss of capital represents the consequence of losing human life through sin. It leads to birth as a denizen of hell or as a brute animal.
Heaven is represented by gain in the merchants' parable and is associated with increasing one's capital through eminent virtues.
Hell is the destination of the great sinner who turns away from the Law and commits unrighteousness. The sinner's pursuit of pleasures is said to gain nothing but life in hell.

The gods possess pleasures that surpass human pleasures a thousand times and more. The virtuous man reaches the state of gods, while one who renounces pleasure believes he will become a god after getting rid of the body.

l: divine life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: Divine life and its pleasures surpass human pleasures a thousand times and more. Losing divine life, as well as human life, leaves a person in states of misery.

l: human pleasures, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: Human pleasures are limited and brief compared with divine pleasures. They are compared to a drop of water at the top of a blade of Kusa-grass when set against the ocean.

l: divine pleasures, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: Divine pleasures surpass human pleasures a thousand times and more. Their superiority shows the smallness of the pleasures available in human life.
A person who has not renounced pleasure misses the true end of the soul and goes astray repeatedly. A person who renounces pleasure does not miss the aim and may attain a godly state.
The Law teaches the consequences of virtue and sin. Following the true Law leads toward the state of gods, while turning away from it leads the great sinner to hell.

l: three merchants, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventh Lecture.
s: The three merchants travel with capital: one gains much, one returns with his capital, and one loses his capital. Their experience is used to explain the Law, with capital meaning human life, gain meaning heaven, and loss meaning birth in hell or as a brute animal.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighth Lecture.
s: This unit presents Kapila's teaching on escaping sorrow and misery in unstable, eternal Samsâra. It instructs a monk to abandon attachment, hatred, pleasures, and killing of living beings, while practicing careful conduct, disciplined almsgiving, meditation, and ascetic practices. It warns that ignorance, lust, worldly desires, and false religious claims lead to sin, rebirth, hell, or birth as Asuras. Those who follow the Law taught by Kapila will be saved and gain both worlds.
Kapila of pure knowledge taught this Law. Those who follow it will be saved and gain both worlds.
Samsâra is unstable, eternal, and full of misery. Pious ascetics (sâdhu) cross it as merchants cross the sea, while sinful beings remain ensnared in it and err through it for a long time.

A monk should abandon former connections, attachment, hatred, pleasures, and desire for women. He should carefully accept suitable alms only for sustaining life, avoid injuring beings, and strictly keep the Law.
A person who fixes his thoughts on the soul's benefit and eternal welfare avoids sinking through hatred and lust. Souls sullied by many sins will hardly ever attain Bôdhi.

l: Law of ascetics, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighth Lecture.
s: The Law of ascetics teaches that killing of living beings should not be permitted and that a monk should practice careful conduct. Kapila taught this Law, and those who follow it will be saved and gain both worlds.
Some who call themselves Sramanas are like ignorant beasts because they do not know the prohibition of killing living beings. Those stupid sinners go to hell through their superstitious beliefs.
Pious ascetics (sâdhu) can get over the impassable Samsâra as merchants cross the sea.

Those who abandon discipline, meditation, and ascetic practices while seeking pleasures, amusements, and good fare will be born again as Asuras. After rising from the world of the Asuras, they err for a long time in Samsâra.

l: living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighth Lecture.
s: Living beings people the world whether they move or not. A monk should do nothing injurious to them in thought, word, or act.
A monk who loves not even those who love him will be freed from sin and hatred. Ignorant sinners who yield to hatred and lust become ensnared and may go to hell.
A monk should cast aside hatred and should not sink through it. A monk who does not love even those who love him will be freed from hatred.
Sinful Karman quits the careful man who does not injure living beings, as water quits raised ground.

l: pleasures and amusements, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighth Lecture.
s: Pleasures are difficult for weak men to cast aside. A monk should not be attached to them, and those who seek pleasures instead of discipline will be born as Asuras.
A monk should not desire women or remain attached to females. Women are described as female demons who entice men and make a sport of them as of slaves.

l: killing of living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighth Lecture.
s: The preceptors who proclaimed the Law of ascetics taught that killing of living beings should not be permitted or consented to. Avoiding it may deliver a person from all misery.
Desires increase with a person's means, and greater possessions produce greater wants. Even when two mâshas would supply a need, a person would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Ninth Lecture.
s: King Nami remembers his former birth, becomes a Svayamsambuddha in the true Law, and retires from the world after placing his son on the throne. When Mithilâ is filled with uproar, Sakra tests Nami by urging him to resume royal duties, pleasures, wealth, punishment, conquest, and sacrifices. Nami rejects these pursuits, praises self-control and austerity, and teaches that conquering oneself is greater than conquering others. Sakra reveals himself, praises Nami's virtues, and Nami takes upon him Sramanahood.

l: King Nami, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Ninth Lecture.
s: King Nami remembers his former birth, becomes a Svayamsambuddha, places his son on the throne, and gives up his kingdom, army, seraglio, and retinue. He rejects Sakra's arguments for royal power, wealth, pleasures, punishment, conquest, and sacrifice, teaching instead the value of self-control, patience, austerity, and conquering oneself. He takes upon him Sramanahood.

Sakra comes to Nami in the guise of a Brâhmana and questions him about the uproar in Mithilâ. He repeatedly urges Nami to resume royal duties and worldly pursuits, but after hearing Nami's answers he reveals his true form, praises Nami, pays reverence to him, and flies up through the air.

Mithilâ is filled with uproar when Nami retires from the world. Nami explains the noise by comparing it to birds screaming when the sacred tree Manôrama is shaken by a storm, and says that when Mithilâ is on fire nothing belonging to him is burned.
Pravragyâ is the excellent stage reached by the royal Seer Nami when he retires from the world. His Pravragyâ causes an uproar in Mithilâ.

l: Nami's enlightenment, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Ninth Lecture.
s: Nami becomes enlightened after enjoying excellent pleasures with the beautiful ladies of his seraglio. He gives up those pleasures and becomes a Svayamsambuddha in the true Law.

l: Nami's retirement from the world, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Ninth Lecture.
s: Nami retires from the world after placing his son on the throne and giving up Mithilâ, his army, seraglio, and retinue. He resorts to a lonely place and takes upon him Sramanahood.

The true Law is the teaching in which Nami becomes a Svayamsambuddha. Nami's answers identify self-control, patience, carefulness, content, truth, austerity, and freedom from worldly ties with the path of the wise.
Nami puts an end to the influence of delusion and remembers his former birth. He teaches that delusion blocks one's path.
Nami enjoys excellent pleasures before becoming enlightened, then gives them up. He teaches that pleasures are thorns, poison, and like a venomous snake, and that desire for them leads to a bad end.
Nami teaches that a sage who uses faith, penance, self-control, patience, zeal, carefulness, content, and truth as spiritual weapons can become victorious and get rid of Samsâra.
Nami describes Karman as the foe's mail that is pierced by the arrow of penance in the sage's spiritual battle.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The unit concerns Gautama and the soul's perilous passage through embodied existence and Samsâra. It teaches that human life and human birth are brief and rare opportunities, and that souls may remain for vast periods in earth, water, fire, wind, vegetable, animal, divine, or hellish bodies. Gautama is urged to abandon attachments, wealth, wife, friends, relations, and carelessness, and to follow the best Law and the great path. The Buddha's well-delivered sermon leads Gautama to cut off love and hatred and reach perfection, the world of safety and perfect happiness.

l: The Leaf of the Tree, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The Leaf of the Tree is the subject of the comparison with a fallow leaf that falls when its days are gone. It illustrates the brevity and ending of human life.

Gautama is repeatedly urged to be careful, wipe off his sins, abandon attachments, and follow the right path. He has entered the houseless state, crossed the great ocean, and, after hearing the Buddha's well-delivered sermon, cut off love and hatred and reached perfection.

l: the soul, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The soul may remain for vast periods in earth, water, fire, wind, or vegetable bodies, and for specified periods in bodies of beings possessing two, three, four, or five organs of sense. It may remain one whole life in the body of a god or a denizen of hell, and through carelessness is driven about in Samsâra by good and bad Karman.

l: human life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: Human life is compared to a fallow leaf and a dew-drop, because it comes to its close quickly and lasts only a short time. Its fleeting and precarious nature is a reason to wipe off sins and practise the Law.

l: human birth, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: Human birth is described as a rare chance in the long course of time for a living being. Even after human birth, becoming an Ârya, possessing all five organs of sense, receiving instruction in the best Law, believing it, and practising it are each described as rare.
Samsâra is the condition through which the careless soul is driven about. Good and bad Karman cause this movement.
Karman is described as good or bad and as driving the careless soul about in Samsâra. The consequences of actions are hard.

The best Law is difficult to encounter even for one who possesses all five organs of sense. People follow heretical teachers, and even those instructed in the right Law rarely believe in it or practise it.

l: the houseless state, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The houseless state is the condition Gautama has entered after giving up his wealth and wife. He is warned not to return to his vomit.

l: the great path, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The great path is the path from which the thorns have been cleared. Gautama is told to walk in the right path and not take an uneven road.

l: the world of perfection, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The world of perfection is reached by going through the same religious practices as perfected saints. It is described as a place of safety and perfect happiness.
The enlightened and liberated monk should control himself in a village or a town. He should preach to all the road of peace.

l: the road of peace, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The road of peace is what the enlightened and liberated monk should preach to all. It is associated with control and liberation.

l: the Buddha, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The text says that there is now no Gina, but there is a highly esteemed guide to show the way. It also refers to the Buddha as the source of a well-delivered sermon.

l: the Buddha's well-delivered sermon, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Tenth Lecture.
s: The Buddha's well-delivered sermon is adorned by illustrations. Having heard it, Gautama cut off love and hatred and reached perfection.
Perfection is reached by Gautama after he cuts off love and hatred. It is associated with the world of safety and perfect happiness.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eleventh Lecture.
s: The Eleventh Lecture explains the right discipline of a houseless monk who has abandoned worldly ties. It identifies causes that make wholesome discipline impossible and qualities that make discipline a virtue. It distinguishes ill-behaved monks from well-behaved monks and praises the superiority, learning, and virtues of a very learned monk. It urges the seeker after the highest truth to study sacred lore so that self and others may attain perfection.

Discipline is impossible because of egoism, delusion, carelessness, illness, and idleness. It is called virtue when accompanied by qualities such as self-control, truthfulness, freedom from covetousness and anger, and avoidance of harmful speech and wrong conduct.

A monk who is ignorant, egoistical, greedy, undisciplined, or loose in speech is ill-behaved, while one who is humble, steady, truthful, receptive to advice, and kind is well-behaved. A very learned monk is praised as superior to others and, after his Karman is annihilated, monks who are deep, fearless, difficult to overcome, learned, and self-controlled go to the highest place.
The seeker after the highest truth is instructed to study the sacred lore in order to cause himself and others to attain perfection.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: Harikêsa-Bala, a monk and sage born in a family of Svapâkas, is assaulted while begging at a Brahmanical sacrifice by young men acting on the Brahmanas’ orders. Bhadrâ identifies him as the ascetic who had refused her after king Kausalika gave her to him, and Yakshas protect him from further harm. The Brahmanas and their followers repent, offer Harikêsa food and drink, and learn from him that true sacrifice consists in self-restraint, non-injury, renunciation, and purity rather than external rites. Gods honor the event and proclaim that penance surpasses birth and caste.

Harikêsa-Bala was born in a family of Svapâkas, became a monk and sage, subdued his senses, and observed the rules of mendicancy. While begging at a Brahmanical sacrifice, he was mocked and beaten, but he remained without hatred, accepted the Brahmanas’ apology and food, and taught them about true sacrifice and purity.

The Brahmanas at the sacrifice mocked Harikêsa, refused him food, and ordered young men to drive him away. After Yakshas protected him, they and their wife Bhadrâ begged his forgiveness, offered him food, and questioned him about the proper method of sacrifice.

l: Brahmanical sacrifice, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: Harikêsa approached the enclosure of a Brahmanical sacrifice while begging. Its priests claimed that the food was prepared exclusively for themselves and used the occasion to reject and assault him.

l: Yaksha of the Tinduka-tree, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: The Yaksha living in the Tinduka-tree took compassion on Harikêsa, made its body invisible, and spoke in his defense. Later, Yakshas came to Harikêsa’s assistance and kept the young men away from him.

Bhadrâ, the daughter of king Kausalika and the Brahmana’s wife, stopped the angry young men and identified Harikêsa as the ascetic who had refused her. She warned that harming a monk would bring ruin, urged the Brahmanas to seek protection, and helped lead them to appease him.

l: king Kausalika, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: King Kausalika had given his daughter Bhadrâ to Harikêsa, but Harikêsa would not accept her.

l: young men, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: At the teachers’ command, many young men beat Harikêsa with sticks, canes, and whips. Yakshas and Asuras then drove them off and caused them to suffer, after which they bowed and sought protection.

l: asking for something, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: Mendicancy requires Harikêsa to beg for food prepared for others, possess nothing, avoid cooking his food, and follow rules concerning walking, begging, speaking, easing nature, and receiving and keeping necessities.
Harikêsa is emaciated by penance, and the gods declare that the value of penance has become visible through his power. He describes penance as his fire in the spiritual sacrifice.

l: birth and caste, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: The Brahmanas rely on pure birth and knowledge to claim superiority, but Harikêsa teaches that angry, violent, lying, thieving, property-owning people are bad fields regardless of their status. The gods proclaim that birth is of no value compared with penance, citing Harikêsa, the son of a Svapâka.

Harikêsa compares the recipient of a gift to a field that may return merit, as farmers sow corn hoping for a return. He teaches that the saints, who call at both high and lowly houses, are blessed fields.
Harikêsa says that the Law is his pond and teaches that living under self-restraint, avoiding injury, lying, taking what is not given, property, women, pride, and deceit is the proper path.

Harikêsa protects his thoughts, speech, and body from sin. He teaches that violence in tending fires and using ritual materials causes living beings to be injured and leads the ignorant to commit sins repeatedly.

Harikêsa is praised as one who subdues his senses and observes self-control. He teaches that self-control, right exertion, and tranquillity are the oblations of the true sacrifice, and that protection by the five Samvaras leads to victory.
Harikêsa identifies Karman as the fuel in his spiritual fire. He teaches that this inner sacrifice is made through penance, right exertion, self-control, and tranquillity.
Harikêsa identifies celibacy as his holy bathing-place, clear and uncontaminated for the soul. In that spiritual bath, he becomes pure and removes hatred or impurity.

l: injury to living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: Harikêsa teaches that the proper sacrifice involves doing no injury to living beings of the six orders. He says that using Kusa-grass, sacrificial poles, straw, and wood, together with ritual actions, injures living beings.
The Brahmanas ask where the monks’ fire and fireplace are and what oblations they offer. Harikêsa answers that penance is his fire, life is his fireplace, and Karman is its fuel.

Harikêsa teaches that self-control, right exertion, and tranquillity are the oblations praised by the sages. He calls abandoning the body in purity and without attachment the great victory and best of offerings.

The Brahmanas use water morning and evening in pursuit of external purity. Harikêsa teaches that such external purity is not the right kind and that true purification comes through the Law, celibacy, and removal of hatred.

l: food and drink, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: The Brahmanas initially refuse Harikêsa the food and drink prepared for them. After seeking forgiveness, they offer him boiled rice seasoned with many condiments and other food and drink, which he accepts after fasting for a whole month.

l: corporal punishment, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twelfth Lecture
s: Harikêsa is mocked by the priests and assaulted by young men with sticks, canes, and whips while on his begging tour. Bhadrâ intervenes, Yakshas and Asuras protect him, and the Brahmanas later apologize for the injury and abuse.
Harikêsa teaches that true bathing occurs in the Law, with celibacy as the clear holy bathing-place. This bathing purifies the soul and removes hatred or impurity, unlike merely washing with water.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirteenth Lecture.
s: This unit concerns Sambhûta, later born as Brahmadatta, and Kitra, who meet again in Kâmpilya and recall their former births and the rewards of their actions. Kitra urges Brahmadatta, king of the Pañkâlas, to abandon sensual pleasures and enter the order, but Brahmadatta refuses. Brahmadatta later sinks into hell, while Kitra practices self-control and reaches the highest place of perfection.

Sambhûta was contemptuously treated because he was a Kândâla and formed a sinful resolution to become a universal monarch in a later birth. He was later born as Brahmadatta and met Kitra again in Kâmpilya.

Kitra was born in Purimatâla in a merchant family and entered the order after hearing the Law. He advised Brahmadatta to abandon sensual pleasures, practiced excellent conduct and penance, and reached the highest place of perfection.
Brahmadatta was Sambhûta reborn as a powerful king of the Pañkâlas. He declined Kitra's counsel, continued enjoying sensual pleasures, and afterwards sank into the deepest hell.
Hastinâpura was where Sambhûta, in a former birth, saw the powerful king Sanatkumâra and formed his sinful resolution out of desire for sensual pleasures.
Kâmpilya was where Brahmadatta and Kitra met again and told each other the rewards they had realized for their good and bad actions.

l: the Pañkâlas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirteenth Lecture.
s: The Pañkâlas were ruled by Brahmadatta, who was called their king and was urged to abandon transitory pleasures.
The Law is known by Brahmadatta, but he does not follow its counsel. Kitra has heard and practiced it, urging compassion, right conduct, and renunciation.
Karman is produced by sinful thoughts and follows the doer into a new existence. It causes separation and determines whether the next existence is good or bad.

l: good actions, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirteenth Lecture.
s: Good actions bear fruit, bringing wealth, prosperity, splendour, and other rewards. The text also presents their practice as necessary for avoiding regret after death.
Sensual pleasures are impermanent, difficult to abandon, and produce pain. Brahmadatta continues to long for them despite knowing the Law, and his attachment contributes to his downfall.
Renunciation is presented as difficult for those attached to sensual pleasures. Kitra urges Brahmadatta to choose it for the sake of the highest good.

l: the order, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirteenth Lecture.
s: The order is the path Kitra entered after hearing the Law and the path he urges Brahmadatta to enter for the highest good.

l: the world of perfection, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirteenth Lecture.
s: The highest place of perfection is reached by Kitra after he practices the highest self-control and remains indifferent to pleasure.
Hell is where Brahmadatta sinks after refusing Kitra's counsel and continuing to enjoy the highest sensual pleasures.

l: the sinful resolution, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirteenth Lecture.
s: The sinful resolution was formed by Sambhûta in Hastinâpura from desire for sensual pleasures and was to become a universal monarch in a later birth.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: The unit concerns Ishukâra, its king and queen, the Brahmanical Purôhita Bhrigu, his wife, and their two sons. The two sons reject Vedic study, household duties, wealth, and pleasures, and choose the path of the Ginas. Bhrigu, his wife, King Ishukâra, and Kamalâvatî successively abandon domestic life and enter the monastic order. They understand that birth, old age, death, and worldly pleasures bind beings to Samsâra, and they all eventually reach perfection and the end of misery.

Ishukâra is an ancient, wealthy, and famous town described as beautiful like heaven. Several beings born there remember former merit, abandon worldly pleasures, and take refuge in the path of the Ginas.

l: king Ishukâra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: King Ishukâra is one of those who abandons his kingdom and pleasures after hearing the Law from Kamalâvatî. He enters the monastic order with her and eventually reaches perfection.
Kamalâvatî is the wife of King Ishukâra. She rejects the world and its pleasures, urges the king to abandon his kingdom and property, and becomes a nun before reaching perfection.

Bhrigu is the Brahmanical Purôhita and the father of two sons who wish to become monks. After his sons enter the order, he recognizes that domestic life has lost its attraction, becomes a mendicant, and eventually reaches perfection.

l: the two sons of Bhrigu, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: The two sons of Bhrigu remember their former birth, penance, and self-control. They reject Vedic study, sacrifices, sons, wealth, and pleasures, enter the monastic order, and reach the end of misery.
Samsâra is feared as the Wheel of Births from which the practitioners seek escape. Attachment to pleasures and wrong actions keep beings within it.
Birth is regarded as part of the precarious and transitory condition of human life. Fear of birth, together with old age and death, motivates the characters to abandon worldly life.
Death harasses mankind, and no one can escape or safely postpone preparation for it. Awareness of death leads the characters to adopt the Law immediately.

l: domestic life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: Domestic life is portrayed as impermanent and unattractive to those seeking liberation. The characters abandon family, property, pleasures, and household responsibilities to become mendicants or a nun.

l: wandering mendicant life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: Monastic life consists of renouncing pleasures and property, practising penance and self-control, wandering, and collecting alms. The characters choose it as the path toward liberation and the end of misery.
Pleasures provide only brief happiness but cause prolonged suffering and obstruct liberation. The characters abandon them because they bind beings to worldly existence.
Liberation is the desired escape from existence and the Wheel of Births. It is pursued through faith, renunciation, the Law, penance, and self-control.
The Law is presented as the only lasting safeguard at death and as the path that prevents rebirth. Those who act according to it gain profit from the passing days and eventually reach perfection.

l: the soul, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: The soul cannot be apprehended by the senses because it has no corporeal form, and it is therefore eternal. Its fetter is caused by bad qualities, which produce worldly existence.

l: worldly existence, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: Worldly existence is caused by the soul's fetter and is continued by attachment to pleasures. The characters seek to end it through renunciation and correct understanding.

l: the world, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: The world is consumed by the fire of love and hatred, while people attached to pleasures fail to perceive this. Its instability and dangers lead the characters to withdraw from it.

l: the end of misery, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fourteenth Lecture.
s: The end of misery is reached by those who overcome doubts about the true doctrine, realise the Bhâvanâs, and practise the Law. The king, queen, Bhrigu, his wife, and his sons all attain it.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifteenth Lecture.
s: This unit describes the conduct and discipline of a true monk who adopts the Law and lives with other monks. He abandons former connections, desire, worldly gain, divination, medical practices, praise, and dependence on householders. He protects his soul from sins, practises austerities and self-discipline, endures hardships, and eats whatever lowly food and drink are given. The unit concludes that a true monk leaves the house, lives single, subdues his senses, and remains sinless.

The monk adopts the Law, lives uprightly with other monks, abandons former connections and desires, and wanders as an unknown beggar. He controls himself, keeps the vows, practises austerities, protects his soul from sins, endures hardships, avoids worldly arts and gain, and lives single without a house or friends.
The Law is adopted by one who intends to live as a monk.
The monk protects his soul from every wrong and meditates on his soul. He does so through self-discipline, restraint, and freedom from attachment.
The monk abstains from sins and always protects his soul from them. He is described as sinless when he subdues his senses and lives without ties.
The monk practises austerities continually, keeps the vows, and endures heat, cold, insects, lowly beds, lodgings, and frightening noises.

The monk does not improve his acquaintance with householders for earthly gain. He takes bed, lodging, drink, food, or dainties from householders only when they give them themselves, and he remains free from anger when they do not.

l: food and drink, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Fifteenth Lecture.
s: A monk may receive food and drink, including dainties and spices, but he must remain disciplined in thoughts, words, and deeds. He should not despise dish-water, barley-pap, cold sour gruel, or water in which barley has been washed, and should call at the lowliest houses for alms.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixteenth Lecture.
s: The Sixteenth Lecture concerns the ten conditions for the realisation of perfect celibacy among monks. Sudharman recounts that Mahâvîra taught how these conditions lead monks to self-discipline, Samvara, contemplation, guarded senses, and faithful observance of religious duties. The rules prohibit unsuitable lodgings, conversation and proximity with women, sensual attention, excessive or refined food, ornaments, and attachment to pleasant sense objects. The concluding verses praise the chaste monk and affirm the eternal Law proclaimed by the Ginas.

l: Sixteenth Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixteenth Lecture.
s: The Sixteenth Lecture presents ten conditions for the realisation of celibacy and verses explaining the same discipline. It concludes by affirming the Law proclaimed by the Ginas.
Mahâvîra is the Venerable teacher whose Discourse Sudharman recounts. His teaching concerns the conditions by which monks preserve chastity and fulfil their religious duties.

The venerable Sthaviras are said to have declared ten conditions for the realisation of celibacy. Hearing and understanding these conditions enables monks to advance in self-discipline, Samvara, contemplation, and guarded conduct.

A Nirgrantha is instructed not to rest in places frequented by women, cattle, or eunuchs, converse with women, share their seat, observe their charms, listen to their sounds behind a barrier, recall past pleasures with them, eat well-dressed food or to excess, wear ornaments, or care for pleasant sense objects. Violating these precautions may lead to doubt about chastity, sensual desire, remorse, broken rules, passion, illness, or desertion of the faith.

Monks who hear and understand the ten conditions are expected to attain greater self-discipline, Samvara, contemplation, sense-guarding, chastity, and attentiveness to religious duties. A chaste monk should live detached, eat in the prescribed manner, avoid sensual pleasures, and remain steadfast in the Law.
Women are described as persons whose company, conversation, appearance, sounds, and past pleasures a monk must avoid. A monk's ornaments may also make him an object of desire to women.

Celibacy is realised through ten conditions involving lodging, speech, proximity, sight, hearing, memory, food, moderation, ornaments, and the five pleasant senses. The text presents these conditions as protection against sensuality and doubts about chastity.

l: places for sleep or rest, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixteenth Lecture.
s: Places for sleep or rest should not be frequented by women, cattle, or eunuchs. Occupying such places may create doubt about a Nirgrantha's chastity or lead to sensual desire, remorse, rule-breaking, passion, illness, or abandonment of the faith.

l: pleasant things, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Sixteenth Lecture.
s: Pleasant things include sounds, colours, smells, tastes, feelings of touch, refined food and drink, ornaments, conversation, company, and looking at women's charms. They are difficult to abandon and are compared to the poison Tâlaputa for one seeking the true Self.

The Law is portrayed as the discipline in which a monk should remain steadfast, content, restrained, and attentive to the duties of chastity. It is called unchangeable, permanent, and eternal; the Ginas proclaimed it, and through it the Siddhas reached perfection.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventeenth Lecture.
s: The Seventeenth Lecture concerns The Bad Sramana and the conduct that makes a religious practitioner bad. It describes a Nirgrantha who, after entering the order, learning the Law, receiving discipline, and obtaining Bôdhi, becomes careless, indulgent, disrespectful, or harmful. It lists many behaviors by which a Sramana is called bad, including neglect of inspection, careless walking and sitting, eating improperly, quarrelling, following heretical teachers, and living by fortune-telling. It concludes that a bad monk is despised like poison, while one who avoids these sins is welcomed like nectar and conquers this world and the next.

l: Seventeenth Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventeenth Lecture.
s: The Seventeenth Lecture teaches about The Bad Sramana. It distinguishes the conduct of a bad monk from that of one who avoids sins and is pious among his brethren.

l: The Bad Sramana, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventeenth Lecture.
s: The Bad Sramana sleeps, eats, and drinks as much as he likes, neglects learning and discipline, disrespects his preceptor and teachers, harms living beings, and acts carelessly. He may be deceitful, talkative, arrogant, greedy, quarrelsome, improperly fed, attached to householders, or devoted to heretical teachers and fortune-telling. He is despised in this world like poison and is nobody in this world and in that beyond.
A Nirgrantha may enter the order, learn the Law, receive religious discipline, and obtain Bôdhi which is difficult to obtain. Afterwards, he may begin to live as he likes and become a bad Sramana.

A Sramana is called bad when he neglects discipline, fails to respect his preceptor and teachers, harms living beings, acts without care, quarrels, indulges in improper eating, or follows other improper practices. A Sramana who avoids these sins and is pious among his brethren is welcomed like nectar and conquers this world and the next.

l: monk (the bad Sramana), Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Seventeenth Lecture.
s: The bad monk does not protect himself from sins like the heretics, although he has the appearance of a monk. He is the lowest among his worthy brethren and is despised in this world like poison.

The sins described include indulgence, neglect of learning and discipline, disrespect, harming living beings, careless inspection and movement, deceit, greed, quarrelling, improper eating, abandoning one's teacher, following heretical ones, fortune-telling, and dependence on householders. One who always avoids these sins is pious among his brethren and conquers this world and the next.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighteenth Lecture.
s: Sañgaya, king of Kâmpilya, encounters a houseless ascetic after killing a deer and is taught the Law. He abandons kingly power and adopts the faith of the Ginas under Gardabhâli. The unit teaches that worldly ties are transient, sinful actions bring punishment, and righteous conduct leads to heaven and perfection. It also recounts many kings who achieved perfection through royal renunciation and entry into the ascetic order.

Sañgaya was king of Kâmpilya and went hunting in the Kêsara-park, where he killed a deer that had fled to a houseless ascetic. Taught the Law by the monk Gardabhâli, he gave up his kingly power and adopted the faith of the Ginas.
Kâmpilya was the town ruled by Sañgaya. Its Kêsara-park was where Sañgaya hunted and encountered the houseless ascetic.

l: houseless ascetic, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighteenth Lecture.
s: The houseless ascetic studied sacred texts, meditated on the Law, and annihilated sinful inclinations. After Sañgaya killed the deer that fled to him, he taught the king about transience, cruelty, Karman, and the need for penance.
Gardabhâli was Sañgaya’s teacher and was conversant with sacred lore and good conduct. Sañgaya adopted the faith of the Ginas in his presence.

The Ginas are presented as the enlightened authorities whose creed teaches the existence of the soul, the consequences of sin, and the path of righteousness. Sañgaya adopted their faith, and the unit names many kings who followed it.

The Law teaches that living beings and worldly possessions are transient, that sinful actions have consequences, and that one should practise penance, righteousness, and self-control. Sañgaya was filled with desire for purity after being taught the Law.

Karman accompanies a person’s good or wicked actions into the next existence. Kings and ascetics are described as hewing down, annihilating, or becoming free from Karman through austerities and renunciation.
Monks are expected to practise self-control, sacred study, austerities, and right conduct. They should abandon heretical doctrines, personal fancies, and deeds productive of evil.

l: kingly power, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighteenth Lecture.
s: Kingly power is portrayed as transient and ultimately something that must be abandoned. Sañgaya and many other kings gave it up and entered the ascetic order.
Bharatavarsha is described as a kingdom or earth-girt realm abandoned by Bharata, Sagara, Maghavan, Sanatkumâra, Sânti, Kunthu, Ara, and others when they renounced worldly life.

The king is warned that wives, children, friends, and relations will not follow him in death, while others may enjoy the riches and wives he leaves behind. A king should therefore practise penance, abandon cruelty, and renounce worldly power.

l: royal renunciation and entry into the ascetic order, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Eighteenth Lecture.
s: Royal renunciation involves placing a son on the throne, abandoning kingdoms, armies, pleasures, and kingly power, and entering the order as a monk or Sramana. The unit gives Sañgaya and numerous other kings as examples of this course.

Perfection is reached by those who renounce the world, practise self-restraint or austerities, and become free from defilement and Karman. The unit says that several named kings and Gaya with thousands of kings reached perfection.

Self-control is the way of life followed by those who reject heretical doctrines, practise austerities, and live according to the true religion. Gaya and other kings renounced the world and practised self-restraint.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: Balasrî, also called Mrigâputra, is the crown-prince of Sugrîva who remembers his former birth as a Sramana and renounces royal pleasures. Despite his parents' warnings about the severe duties and suffering of the Sramana order, he receives their permission, gives up his wealth and possessions, and enters the order. He practises the Law through vows, self-control, penance, and meditation, purifies himself, and reaches liberation after many years.

Balasrî is the son of King Balabhadra and Mrigâ, the crown-prince of Sugrîva. After remembering his former birth, he rejects pleasures, renounces his property, enters the Sramana order, and practises austerities until he reaches perfection.
A Sramana is described as practising penance, self-restraint, self-control, and virtue. Mrigâputra becomes a Sramana who is impartial, detached, and free from property and egoism.

l: the monastic order, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: The Sramana order requires difficult duties, including impartiality, abstention from injury, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, non-possession, fasting rules, and endurance of hardship. Mrigâputra enters the order after his parents permit him to do so.

l: five great vows, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: The five great vows are among the demanding duties of a Sramana. Mrigâputra observes them after entering the order.

The Law is followed to avoid suffering in the next world and to become exempt from Karman and suffering. Mrigâputra practises it through self-control, penance, right conduct, faith, knowledge, and pure meditation.
Samsâra is described as a large ocean, a mine of dangers, and a wilderness of old age and death. Mrigâputra says he has repeatedly undergone dreadful births, deaths, misery, and dangers in it.
Karman is the cause of bondage and suffering. Mrigâputra prevents its influx through bad channels and becomes exempt from it through observance of the Law and self-purification.
Nirvâna is the great happiness toward which the Law leads. Mrigâputra reaches perfection and liberation, described as famous in the three worlds.

Hell contains suffering from extreme heat and cold, roasting, cutting, crushing, burning, piercing, and other punishments. Mrigâputra remembers having undergone these sufferings infinitely many times and says they are far worse than suffering in the human world.

l: former birth, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: While looking at a restrained Sramana, Mrigâputra remembers his former birth and recognizes that he had previously been a Sramana. This remembrance causes him to reject pleasures and seek renunciation.

l: Mrigâputra's renunciation, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: Mrigâputra renounces his power, wealth, friends, wives, sons, relations, and all claims to property after obtaining his parents' permission. He then goes forth, observes the great vows, and lives without attachment or egoism.

l: Mrigâputra's liberation, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: Mrigâputra purifies himself through knowledge, right conduct, faith, penance, and pure meditations. After living many years as a Sramana and breaking his fast only once every month, he reaches perfection and liberation.

A wild animal roams and lives by itself in forests, finds its own food and drink, and receives no one to cure or feed it when sick. Mrigâputra uses this life as an example for the independent life of a monk.
The body is described as impermanent, impure, transitory, and a vessel of suffering. Mrigâputra says he takes no delight in it because it must eventually be left behind.
Pleasures are compared to poisonous or Kimpâka fruit whose consequences are painful. Mrigâputra gives them up after reflecting on their connection with continuous suffering.

Suffering occurs in birth, old age, disease, death, Samsâra, and especially hell. Mrigâputra recalls experiencing bodily and mental suffering countless times and seeks freedom from it through the Law.

l: the flood of old age and death, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: Old age and death are portrayed as consuming the world and making Samsâra a wilderness of danger. Their threat motivates Mrigâputra to save himself through renunciation and the Law.

l: parents' permission, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Nineteenth Lecture.
s: Mrigâputra's parents warn him that Sramana duties are extremely difficult, but ultimately grant permission for him to enter the order. After making them repeat their permission, he gives up his property and goes forth.
Mrigâputra observes the five great vows, five Samitis, and three Guptis, and practises mental and bodily penance. He meditates, purifies himself, and breaks his fast only once every month.
Mrigâputra gives up his fields, house, gold, power, wealth, servants, family claims, and all other property. He renounces possessions permanently, as a snake casts off its slough.
